extracted.intended_audience: MIT researchers, inventors, faculty, students, and staff involved in technology commercialization
extracted.subtask_description: An institutional inventor guide describing MIT's policies and practical steps for technology transfer: disclosure, assessment, protection (patents/copyright/trademark), marketing, licensing, start-up formation, conflict-of-interest, and revenue distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology Transfer Defined (formal licensing)
rubrics_metrics.description: For this guide, technology transfer refers to the formal licensing of technology to third parties, under the guidance of professionals employed by universities, research foundations and businesses, in departments focused on these activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology transfer can also occur informally (publications, students, conferences), but the guide focuses on formal license-based transfers. Licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may be limited by field-of-use and/or geography.

rubrics_metrics.name: 10 Steps to Commercialization (process checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequenced set of typical steps: 1) Research; 2) Pre-disclosure; 3) Invention Disclosure; 4) Assessment; 5) Protection; 6) Marketing; 7a) Form a Start-up; 7b) Existing Business Relationship; 8) Licensing; 9) Commercialization; 10) Revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps may vary in sequence and overlap. Each step includes responsibilities for inventors and the TLO (e.g., disclose early, assist with marketing, file patents, license negotiations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention Disclosure (what and when to submit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Technology Disclosure (Invention Disclosure) is a written description of your invention provided to the TLO; it should list sponsors and note dates of any upcoming or prior public disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit whenever you have discovered something unique with possible commercial value, and well before public communications (publications, posters, abstracts, theses). The Disclosure is treated as 'MIT Confidential' and should fully document the invention to enable evaluation and protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of Disclosure vs Public Disclosure (patent preservation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete and submit the Technology Disclosure Form in sufficient time to file a patent application before publicly disclosing your technology or publishing a manuscript—preferably before submitting the manuscript for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public disclosure can restrict or eliminate patent rights outside the U.S.; contact TLO before any external discussions. If a patent application has not been filed, TLO can provide an NDA for external discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-Disclosure Consultation with TLO
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact the Technology Licensing Office during your discovery process to learn options that best leverage commercial potential and get guidance on disclosure, evaluation, and protection processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO assists on marketability, funding, partners, patenting, start-up considerations, MIT policies, and can help with NDAs and MTAs. Early contact increases chances for effective protection and commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment Criteria for Invention Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO reviews novelty, competing technologies, protectability and marketability, relationship to related IP, size and growth potential of the relevant market, time and money required for further development, pre-existing rights, and potential competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment may include patent searches and market/competitive analyses. Evaluation guides strategy (license to existing company vs start-up). Consider whether IP can support a start-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection Decision Factors (whether to file patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection (commonly patenting) is pursued to encourage third-party interest; decision considers commercial potential and may require significant investment over years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO and inventor discuss factors; TLO makes final decision whether to file. Patents are expensive; TLO carefully reviews commercial potential before investing. Other protections include copyright and trademark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents: What They Provide (scope of rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent gives the holder the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, offering to sell, and importing any patented invention; patent claims legally define the protectable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent does not necessarily provide an affirmative right to practice a technology (others' broader patents may block practice). Claims determine the scope of protection; inventors must work with counsel during drafting and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter includes processes, machines, compositions of matter, articles, some computer programs, and methods (including methods of making compositions and methods of performing business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturally occurring substances are not patentable in their natural state, but isolated or significantly modified forms may be, if adequately novel and non-obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship Definition and Determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Under U.S. law, an inventor is a person who takes part in the conception of the ideas in the patent claims; inventorship may change as claims change during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination can be intricate and may require counsel. Employers or funders are not inventors. Inventors are asked to sign Inventor's Declarations and Assignments at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patenting Process and Prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications are drafted by patent counsel/agent; after filing, the PTO examines and issues Office Actions; prosecution involves responses, claim amendments, and may require multiple cycles before allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor input is often needed during prosecution. Applications are confidential until PTO publication (typically 18 months). 'Patent pending' is the period between filing and grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional vs Utility (regular) Application Differences
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional application is not examined and does not require claims; it can preserve an earlier filing date but a regular application must be filed within one year to claim benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional filings can temporarily reduce costs and buy time, but adequate description/enabling disclosure is required to get the effective filing date benefit; attorney involvement may still be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Patent Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patent protection is governed by each country's laws; most foreign countries will lose patent rights if the invention is publicly disclosed before filing a priority application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. has a one-year grace period after publication; many other countries do not. Use PCT or timely national filings to preserve foreign rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT (Patent Cooperation Treaty) Advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT provides a streamlined filing procedure for many industrialized nations, delaying costly foreign filings (typically to 30 months) and providing an international preliminary examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a PCT can simplify foreign prosecution and delay expense while the invention is evaluated or marketed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline and Costs of Patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Average U.S. utility patent pendency is about three years (longer in biotech/computer fields); patents are enforceable for 20 years from initial filing (subject to maintenance fees). Filing and obtaining patents can cost tens of thousands of dollars (e.g., $10,000–$20,000 to file, similar sums for prosecution; foreign costs often exceed $20,000 per country).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors should plan for significant time and monetary investments; maintenance fees apply after grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who Decides What Gets Patented
rubrics_metrics.description: The Technology Licensing Office and the inventor(s) discuss relevant factors in deciding whether to file; ultimately, the Technology Licensing Office makes the final decision to file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO aims to balance commercial potential, costs, and institutional objectives; inventors provide technical input and market contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Inventions and Inter-Institutional Ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: When inventions are created with another institution or company, ownership is generally joint; each inventor assigns rights to their employer, and institutions typically make inter-institutional agreements on management, expenses, and revenue sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often one institution will take the lead in protection and licensing; TLO will negotiate with the other institution to allocate responsibilities and revenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reassignment of Inventions to Inventors (conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If TLO decides not to pursue patent protection or market an invention, MIT may reassign ownership to the inventor(s) upon request, although reassignment of government-funded inventions requires government approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon reassignment inventors are responsible for prior patent costs and future expenses; MIT may require inventors to share future revenues, and may reassert ownership if MIT resources are later used for further development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and Transfer of Research Materials (MTAs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using materials from others requires documentation of date and conditions; incoming Material Transfer Agreements (MTAs) should be completed. Sharing materials with outside collaborators requires outgoing MTAs to document terms of use and protect IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact TLO for MTA assistance. Improper material transfers can endanger IP rights; document conditions and dates carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) for External Discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent application has not been filed, TLO can provide an NDA to protect confidentiality when describing the invention to external parties during evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid external discussions before filing unless covered by an NDA; TLO enters into NDAs for MIT proprietary information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership Determination Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership depends on the employment status of creators, use of MIT facilities/resources, source of funds, and terms of any related agreements; generally MIT owns inventions by its employees made under MIT grants/contracts or using MIT resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, contact TLO. Consulting inventions and inventions created off MIT premises may have different ownership depending on contract terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing Contributors on Disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: All contributors to the ideas leading to a discovery should be mentioned in the Technology Disclosure, even if they are not MIT employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO and legal counsel will determine rights of such persons and institutions. Discuss working relationships with TLO before collaborations begin to understand implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start-up Formation Decision Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice to form a start-up is a joint decision by TLO and inventors; key factors include development risk, development costs versus expected investment return, potential for multiple products, competitive advantage and target market size, and potential revenues sufficient to sustain the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO assists founders with planning, investors, and resources. Founders should have personal agreements reviewed by counsel for taxation and liability implications. TLO negotiates licenses with representatives who are not MIT employees to avoid conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing and How Licensees Are Found
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO identifies candidate companies through inventor contacts, TLO relationships, market research, industry events, publications, and presentations; studies show ~70% of licensees are known to inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor involvement and contacts significantly improve marketing success. The inventor and TLO should work as a team to present the invention to potential licensees.

rubrics_metrics.name: License Agreement Purpose and Selection Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is permission to use IP; licensees are chosen based on their ability to commercialize the technology for the benefit of the general public. License agreements typically require licensees to diligently seek commercialization and provide a reasonable return to MIT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A license may be exclusive, non-exclusive, or exclusive by field-of-use/geography. Licensing terms often include performance milestones and financial terms (fees, royalties, equity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Agreements Related to Tech Transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter-Institutional Agreements, Option Agreements, Option Clauses in Sponsored Research Agreements, Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs), Material Transfer Agreements (MTAs), and Research Agreements are common ancillary agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option agreements can preserve a third party's opportunity to negotiate a license; MTAs govern sharing of materials and can affect IP; OSP handles sponsored research agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor–Licensee Relationship and Time Commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensees typically need inventor assistance ranging from infrequent informal contacts to formal consulting; start-up involvement can require substantial inventor time and is governed by conflict-of-interest policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify roles up front and consult MIT conflict-of-interest and conflict-of-commitment policies as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization Activities (what licensees do)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercialization often involves further development, regulatory approvals, sales and marketing, support, training, documentation, benchmarking tests, prototyping for manufacturability, and performance demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor participation varies; licensees typically invest in reducing technical and market risks to enable product adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: License Performance Milestones and Termination
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses typically include performance milestones that, if unmet, can result in termination, allowing subsequent licensing to another business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milestones protect public benefit and encourage active development; delays and practical considerations can nonetheless hinder re-licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue Types and Realistic Expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses can produce license fees, royalties, and equity; most licenses do not yield substantial revenues—only a small percentage produce large returns (e.g., study: 1% yield over $1M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial returns can take years; equity yields value only upon liquidity events. Non-financial benefits (public impact, relationships) are also important outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue Distribution Policy (inventor shares)
rubrics_metrics.description: Per MIT policy, revenues from license fees, royalties, and equity—minus unreimbursed patenting expenses—are shared with inventors. The inventors' share of royalties is divided equally among all inventors unless inventors agree otherwise in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity received by MIT under a license is distributed to inventors not receiving equity directly from the licensee under the same distribution rules. Inventors receiving equity directly from a licensee do not receive MIT's equity share. License revenues are generally taxable and reported on Form 1099.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Interest Definition and When to Seek Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: A conflict of interest arises when a MIT employee's outside relationship could influence MIT business/research for financial gain, adversely affect research/teaching responsibilities, or provide improper advantage to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek guidance from OSP and/or TLO when uncertain—particularly when submitting research proposals and when considering licenses/options/MTAs involving companies in which you have equity or management interests. Disclose and document outside arrangements per MIT policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Commitment Concerns and Management
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict of commitment arises when outside duties associated with technology licenses or business arrangements negatively impact the ability to meet MIT employment obligations or exceed available time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose arrangements to department heads and consult TLO/OSP; management may include limiting roles or documentation to ensure MIT responsibilities are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and Trademark Basics for MIT IP
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects original works fixed in a tangible medium (including software); trademark/service mark protects symbols/names used in commerce to identify source of goods/services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright is automatic upon fixation; MIT recommends using a copyright notice for MIT-owned works. Trademarks become protected by use in commerce; federal registration provides presumptive nationwide rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: TLO Decision to Proceed Without Identified Licensee (risk acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: MIT may accept the risk of filing a patent application before a licensee is identified; after licensing, the licensee often assumes patenting expenses. MIT may decline further prosecution after a reasonable period of attempting to find a licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing without an identified licensee is sometimes necessary because protection usually precedes finding a licensee; however, continued prosecution depends on prospects for commercialization and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open Source/Software Licensing Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO generally supports open-sourcing software when developers choose to 'give their programs away,' provided MIT retains the right to distribute and open-sourcing is consistent with third-party obligations (e.g., sponsors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are many forms of open-source licensing; contact TLO for advice on appropriate notices and compliance with obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and Responsiveness During Patent/Licensing Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors should respond to TLO and outside patent counsel requests and keep TLO informed of upcoming publications or company interactions related to the IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide company contacts on the Disclosure form; inventor contacts are highly valuable for licensing (70% of licenses executed with companies known to the inventor). Timely responsiveness helps efficient prosecution and marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinvestment of License Revenues into Research and Education
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing revenues received by MIT are shared and reinvested in additional research and education to support further research, researchers, and entrepreneurship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinvestments support creation of new research projects, educational opportunities, and collaborative investments that further MIT's mission.
